tagline: Two Cascade passes link wagon routes, lava fields, rivers and forests.
intro: The McKenzie Pass–Santiam Pass Scenic Byway makes an 82-mile loop across two Cascade passes, through lava fields and forests. Lodgepole pines prevail on the drier east side; Douglas fir and red cedar grow west of the crest. ODOT allows three to five hours and identifies the volcanic and glacial landscapes as nationally significant features of the drive. The route became a National Scenic Byway in 1998.

At McKenzie Pass, today’s highway follows a wagon route cut through lava beds. That difficult crossing sent most early travelers to alternate Cascade routes. In 1935, the Civilian Conservation Corps completed Dee Wright Observatory at the pass, building a shelter from lava found on the site.

Beginning in Sisters, take the loop west over Santiam Pass, then south along the McKenzie River valley toward Clear Lake. Continue south past the river’s waterfalls before turning east on OR 242 toward Proxy Falls and McKenzie Pass. Deadhorse Grade gains nearly 1,200 feet in less than four miles through hairpin turns in this direction. McKenzie Pass stands at 5,325 feet, with lava surrounding the road; Windy Point opens onto a 65-square-mile lava flow. Beyond the lava at the summit, the highway returns to Sisters.

moments.title: Clear Lake
moments.text: Clear Lake’s water takes a long route from mountain to lake. Snow runoff from Mount Washington and nearby terrain supplies most of it, filtering through caverns for more than twenty years before arriving. Below the surface is another measure of time: upright trees stand submerged 100 feet deep, killed approximately 3,000 years ago when volcanic activity formed the lake. Water stays between 35 and 43 degrees Fahrenheit year-round, preserving the submerged trees. The lake forms the McKenzie River’s headwaters; water leaving its southern end goes on to Sahalie and Koosah falls.

moments.title: Proxy Falls
moments.text: At Proxy Falls, the water’s disappearance is part of the story. The main drop is 226 feet, descending from a hanging valley shaped by glaciers 6,000 years ago. Proxy and Upper Proxy falls plunge from glacier-cut cliffs, with lava fields surrounding them on a valley floor filled by eruptions from nearby cinder cones. The falling water sinks through porous ground, leaving the impression of a pool without a surface outlet. An unpaved 1.6-mile loop from OR 242 passes through lava fields and conifer forest, with viewpoints toward both waterfalls.

moments.title: Dee Wright Observatory
moments.text: Dee Wright Observatory turns rough lava into a frame for the Cascade peaks. The open shelter was built with basaltic andesite gathered at the construction site. Its viewing holes isolate individual mountains, while a bronze peak finder on the roof helps identify the surrounding summits and geological features. A Civilian Conservation Corps crew completed the structure in 1935 and named it for its foreman, who had died the previous year. Beside it, the paved half-mile Lava River Interpretive Trail leads through lava gutters and crevasses, with panels explaining their geology.
moments.notice: The lava-stone viewing holes frame individual Cascade peaks.

practical: Dee Wright Observatory: ODOT lists McKenzie Pass as closed by snow from November to July; its suggested visiting season is July–October. (checked 2026-10-11)
